title: The scrubber cannot be told a username, because it refuses a value under twelve characters
foundBy: session agent working in the tour repository, which records and replays a three member campaign through cs-vcr, while building a gate that refuses a recording holding anything of the recorder

evidence.verified: go test ./internal/cassette/ -run TestScrub -count=20 and go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestScrub -count=20: PASS. The reproduction in this record, run against bin/cs-vcr, gave `found 4 env:WHO` and exit status 4, where it had said `WHO was not looked for`. `cs-vcr cassette scrub --recorder` over the committed cassettes, with a real identity, reported every one clean.

resolution: A named value under 12 characters is matched as a whole word, and `--recorder` names the caller without any variable being exported.
details:
With `--from-env VAR`, the `cs-vcr cassette scrub` command is told to find the literal value of a variable. A value under twelve characters is refused with `was not looked for: under 12 characters, so it would match ordinary text`. The scrubber carries on and reports the cassette clean of it.

The reason is sound, and it leaves a gap. A sandbox gives its guest the username of whoever launched it. So the recorder's username is the personal value most likely to be in a cassette. Usernames are short. In one recorded campaign the username was in 51 files of a cassette that the scrubber reported `clean`. It appeared as `home/<name>/hello-app` with no leading slash, and as `/tmp/<name>-verify.js`, which an agent had made up. A capture rule written for `/home/<name>` matches neither.

The scrubber also has no way to learn the recorder's git name or hostname unless they are passed the same way. Both reach a cassette when an agent prints its git configuration, which the sandbox record SBX-043 describes.

Matching a short value as a whole word would avoid the ordinary-text problem the limit guards against. A flag that adds the recorder's own username, git name, git address and hostname to the search would make the common case one command.

The tour's gate does this outside cs-vcr today, with `grep -rlwF` over the cassette for each of those values.

To reproduce, add `drwxr-xr-x 2 alovelace alovelace 4096 .` to a request in any cassette, then run `WHO=alovelace cs-vcr cassette scrub <name> --from-env WHO`.

notes.text: Both requests shipped, with two limits the record did not ask for. A value under 3 characters is still refused. So is a word the API itself uses, such as `user`, `system` or `root`, however it was named. Every request holds `"role":"user"`, so a recorder whose login is `user` would have `--force` rewrite the protocol. Both refusals are reported, as the 12 character one was.

The filer should know the names. The flag is `--recorder`, and it looks for the username, the hostname, and git `user.name` and `user.email`. Findings are reported as `recorder:username` and so on, and `--force` writes `<USER>`, `<HOST>`, `<NAME>` and `<EMAIL>`. A short value matches on `\\b` boundaries, which treats `_` as part of a word, as `grep -w` does. SPEC rule R50a holds the contract.
